items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what is 'visibility'?
choices: The degree to which decision-makers actually know your work happened, independent of whether it was good
How often you talk about yourself in meetings
A formal title reflecting your seniority
How many people follow your work on an internal social feed
items.explanation: Visibility is about whether the people who make decisions about your work actually know it happened — it's separate from the work's quality and separate from how often you personally announce it.
items.reference:
Visibility
decision-makers know the work happened
independent of the work's quality

Why: Elena couldn't argue for Priya not because the work was weak, but because Elena had nothing to cite.
items.learnMore:
Visibility vs. quality

These are two separate variables, and it's easy to conflate them because good work usually feels like it should be self-evidently visible.

QualityVisibility
Determined byThe work itselfWhether it reached a decision-maker
Travels on its own?N/ANo — needs a mechanism

Common mistake

Assuming great work is automatically visible. Priya's fix was excellent and still nearly invisible at calibration — quality doesn't create its own distribution.

That Priya should have waited for a performance review instead of doing the work at all

items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what makes something read as 'self-promotion' rather than simple visibility?
choices: Declaring your own value directly, often in the first person, especially when frequent or unsupported by anything the listener can check
Mentioning your own work at all, under any circumstances
Working on high-impact projects rather than routine ones
Being promoted faster than your peers
items.explanation: Self-promotion specifically means declaring your own value in a way the listener can't verify — it's the first-person, unsupported, frequent claim that causes the boastful read, not the mere fact of being known for your work.
items.reference:
Self-promotion
declaring your own value
unsupported, first-person, frequent

Why: Marcus tells Elena about every piece of work directly — the frequent, unsupported first-person claim is what risks the boastful read.
items.learnMore:
Declaration vs. evidence

The same fact can be phrased as a declaration about yourself or as evidence about the world.

DeclarationEvidence
"I'm the reason checkout works now""Checkout incidents: 3/quarter → 0"
Asks listener to trust self-assessmentGives listener a checkable fact

Common mistake

Treating any mention of your own work as self-promotion. It's the unsupported, first-person framing that causes the cost, not the mention itself.

Marcus's work is objectively worse than Priya's, which makes any mention of it inappropriate
Mentioning work in a 1:1 is always inappropriate regardless of frequency
Standups are not an appropriate venue for any project updates
items.explanation: The unit's concern isn't which venue Marcus uses — it's that repeated, first-person, unverified claims about his own value are what create the boastful read, independent of where they're said.

declaring your own value
unsupported, first-person, frequent

items.prompt: What is 'evidence-based visibility,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Making the work itself, or a record of it, visible instead of declaring your role in it verbally
Only becoming visible after being explicitly asked to present your work
Visibility achieved purely through job title or tenure
Sharing metrics only with your direct manager and no one else
items.explanation: Evidence-based visibility is specifically about letting a record — a doc, a metric, a linked ticket — carry the information, rather than a verbal, first-person declaration of your own value.
items.reference:
Evidence-based visibility
the record carries the information
not a verbal, first-person claim

Why: Priya's running doc — dated, factual, checkable — is what finally gave Elena something to cite.
items.learnMore:
What makes a record 'evidence'

A record counts as evidence when a reader could, in principle, verify it — not because of its length or formatting.

Common mistake

Writing a doc full of "I'm proud of" and self-assessment adjectives. That's a declaration wearing a document's formatting, not evidence.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest example of evidence-based visibility, as opposed to a declaration?
choices: "Checkout incident rate: 3/quarter → 0/quarter after root-causing the connection-pool bug. Writeup: [link]."
"I'm really proud of how I handled the checkout outages this quarter."
"I basically saved checkout single-handedly this quarter."
"I've been working really hard lately and think it's finally paying off."
items.explanation: The first option states a checkable fact with a linked source — evidence a reader could verify. The others ask the listener to accept a personal, unsupported self-assessment.

items.prompt: According to L1, what are the two instinctive but failing modes most people default to?
choices: Stay quiet and hope the work speaks for itself, or speak up frequently and risk sounding like you're campaigning
Work harder, or work smarter
Ask for a promotion directly, or wait to be offered one
Document everything, or document nothing
items.explanation: L1 frames the core tension as silence (invisible, but not boastful) versus loud declaration (visible, but socially costly) — both lose, which is exactly why a third path is needed.
items.reference:
Two failing modes
Silent — no record to cite
Loud — reads as boastful

Why: The unit's whole point is a third option that avoids both costs.
items.learnMore:
Two ways to lose

Silence and loud declaration fail for different reasons, which is exactly why neither is 'the safe option' — they trade one cost for the other.

ModeWhat it costs
Stay quietNo record a decision-maker can cite
Declare loudlyReads as boastful, costs social credibility

Common mistake

Assuming silence is the 'humble,' costless default. It has a real cost too — it's just a cost that shows up later, in a room you're not in.

Because both approaches take exactly the same amount of time to execute
Because most managers actively punish any employee who documents their own work
Because only Priya's specific personality makes both approaches fail
items.explanation: Each mode fails for a different reason — one produces no evidence, the other produces evidence at a social cost — which is exactly why the unit looks for tactics that get evidence without the cost.

items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what is a 'decision point'?
choices: A specific moment when someone with authority is actively forming a judgment your work is relevant to
Any Monday morning standup, regardless of what's being discussed
The moment you personally decide to ask for a promotion
A synonym for 'performance review,' with no other meaning
items.explanation: A decision point is defined narrowly as a moment when a decision-maker is actively forming a relevant judgment — a planning meeting, a calibration cycle, a postmortem review — not just any recurring meeting.
items.reference:
Decision point
a moment a judgment is actively forming
e.g. calibration, planning, a postmortem review

Why: Priya's one-pager landed a week before calibration — timing is what made the same information count more.
items.learnMore:
Not every meeting is a decision point

A decision point is specifically a moment someone with authority is actively forming a judgment your work bears on — a routine status meeting usually isn't one.

Common mistake

Treating timing as a minor detail. The same true information can be nearly wasted at the wrong moment and decisive at the right one — Priya's one-pager is the same content the running doc already held.

items.prompt: Why does sharing the same true information near a decision point matter more than sharing it at a random moment?
choices: Because a decision-maker is actively looking for exactly that kind of input at that moment, not because the information itself changed
Because information becomes more factually accurate the closer it is to a deadline
Because managers only read messages sent in the same week as a meeting
Because the information is legally required to be disclosed near decision points
items.explanation: Timing doesn't change the content — it changes whether a decision-maker is actively looking for exactly that input at the moment it arrives, which is what makes it count for more.

items.prompt: According to L2, why couldn't Elena win the argument in calibration just by sincerely believing Priya did great work?
choices: Every manager in the room has an equally sincere belief in their own reports; what separates winning arguments is what each manager can point to that others can verify
Elena's belief was insincere and she was secretly biased against Priya

Sincere belief is always sufficient in calibration, but Elena forgot to state hers clearly
items.explanation: L2's mechanism is that calibration is a room full of equally sincere claims — what separates a winning argument from a losing one is something citable, not the strength of any one manager's belief.
items.reference:
The advocate-in-the-room problem
an argument is only as strong as what's citable
belief alone is indistinguishable from every other manager's belief

Why: This is the mechanism L2 exists to establish before introducing the four tactics.
items.learnMore:
Why citable beats sincere

In a room full of managers each advocating for their own reports, sincerity is the one thing every manager already has in equal supply — it can't be what separates a winning case from a losing one.

Sincere beliefCitable evidence
Equal across every manager in the roomVaries — this is what actually differentiates cases

items.reference:
Two axes
visibility (low/high)

Why: Raising visibility alone, without managing perception, just trades invisibility for the boastful failure mode.
items.learnMore:
Why one axis isn't enough

"Be more visible" sounds like a single dial, but it collapses two different things: whether people know, and how they read the fact that they know. A person can be highly visible and still read as insufferable.

Common mistake

Treating visibility as a single dial to turn up. Turning it up via first-person declaration just trades invisibility for the boastful failure mode.

Because only senior engineers are allowed to be visible
items.explanation: L2's point is that visibility and its perception are two separate axes — raising visibility alone, without attention to how it reads, risks landing in the 'visible but reads as self-promotion' cell instead of the target cell.

items.reference:
Four tactics

2. Letting others amplify
3. Sharing credit, staying visible as driver

items.prompt: Why does the same claim land as more credible when a peer says it about you than when you say it yourself?
choices: A listener assumes a third party has less self-interested reason to make the claim, compared to the person it's about
Peers are legally required to only say true things about coworkers
Peers always have more complete information than the person themselves
It doesn't actually matter who says it — credibility is identical either way
items.explanation: The mechanism is about perceived self-interest: a listener discounts a self-interested source more than an apparently disinterested one, even when the underlying claim is identical.
items.reference:
Letting others amplify
third party = perceived as less self-interested
same fact, more credible source

Why: This is why Sam mentioning Priya's fix unprompted carries more weight than Priya saying it herself.
items.learnMore:
Why the source changes the reading

The same fact, said by different people, is trusted differently — not because the fact changes, but because the listener weighs the source's apparent self-interest.

SourcePerceived self-interest
You, about your own workHigh
A peer, unpromptedLow

Common mistake

Soliciting the amplification directly. That reintroduces self-interest into the chain and can be detected, undercutting the whole point of a third-party voice.

items.prompt: What is the core idea behind 'letting others amplify' as a tactic?

Directly instructing a coworker to say positive things about you in meetings
Hiring a public relations consultant to promote your internal reputation
Only ever discussing your work when someone else brings it up first, and refusing to answer if they don't
items.explanation: The tactic is about making the underlying evidence available and genuine, not soliciting praise — a solicited version undermines the exact credibility the tactic depends on.

items.prompt: According to L2, why does naming a collaborator's specific contribution alongside your own make your own claim more credible, not less?
choices: It signals the account is accurate rather than self-serving, since a purely self-serving account would tend to omit others' contributions
It legally protects you from accusations of taking too much credit
It makes the statement shorter and therefore easier to believe
It has no effect on credibility either way — it's purely a courtesy
items.explanation: L2 argues that naming someone else's real contribution is a costly signal of accuracy — a purely self-serving account would tend not to volunteer credit to someone else, so doing so makes the whole account read as more trustworthy.
items.reference:
Credit-sharing
"I led X, and Sam's Y caught the issue"
names both roles — reads as accurate, not self-serving

Why: This is what separates the strong version of Priya's all-hands update from both weak extremes.
items.learnMore:
Naming credit as a signal

Volunteering someone else's real contribution is a small cost a purely self-serving account wouldn't pay — which is exactly why paying it makes the rest of the account more believable.

Common mistake

Thinking that naming a collaborator dilutes your own credit. In practice it does the opposite — it's what makes your own claimed role believable rather than suspect.

items.prompt: What problem does saying only 'we fixed the checkout issue' create, according to L2's credit-sharing table?

items.explanation: L2's table pairs two weak extremes: 'we' erases the speaker's own specific role (back to invisibility), while an 'I, single-handedly' framing erases the collaborator's contribution — the strong version names both.
